The KOKKOS port splits the two terms into independent helpers and only the Coulomb one learned about EPS_EWALD_SQR: compute_fpair (lines 194-211) and compute_evdwl (291-307) unconditionally do 'const KK_FLOAT rsq = rsq_in + static_cast<KK_FLOAT>(EPSILON); const KK_FLOAT r2inv = 1.0/rsq;' with EPSILON = 1.0e-20 (line 54), and they receive neither factor_coul nor any flag, so they cannot branch; meanwhile compute_fcoul does get it right, returning 'forcecoul / (rsq_cs + static_cast<KK_FLOAT>(EPS_EWALD_SQR))' at line 264. EPS_EWALD_SQR = 1.0e-12 (line 56), so for a special-bonded pair inside the coulomb cutoff the LJ r6inv differs from the CPU by (1e-12/1e-20)^3 = 1e24, exactly the 24 orders the finding claims. Practical impact is genuinely small: the divergence only appears for rsq comparable to or below 1e-12 (r < 1e-6), and typical core/shell inputs use special_bonds lj/coul 0 0 0 so factor_lj multiplies the LJ term to zero -- but that is also where the risk lies, because under a KK_FLOAT = float build r6inv = 1e60 overflows to inf and inf*0 is NaN, whereas the CPU's 1e36 stays finite in double.

EPS_EWALD_SQR : 0.0);' before r2inv, matching src/CORESHELL/pair_lj_cut_coul_long_cs.cpp:126.
